prompt.context: TTP Specialty is a specialty insurance carrier. They provide niche insurance coverage for non-traditional risks such as damage to oil tankers, pollution, medical malpractice, and injuries to professional athletes. Over the past 3 years, they have set and met aggressive growth targets by doubling their premium written annually. However, they have also seen their profits decline by 50% to $10 million in spite of this growth. They've hired us to diagnose their profitability problem.
prompt.question: Diagnose TTP Specialty's profitability problem and recommend how they can increase profits to $40 million annually within the next two years.

clarifying_info.q: How do insurance companies make money?
clarifying_info.a: Insurance companies make money in two ways: (1) collecting more money in premium than they pay in claims, and (2) earning interest on their assets held.
TTP is only in the US. Headquartered in Philadelphia, PA with underwriters spread across the US.
TTP's customers are wide-ranging: city/state governments, federal agencies, hospitals, professional sports organizations, and oil drillers are some of their biggest clients.
There are 5 major specialty players in the US. They have not experienced the same profitability decline.
In 2016 TTP collected $1 billion in premiums and made a profit of $10 million.

exhibits.title: TTP Revenue and Costs 2014-2016
exhibits.shows: A table showing TTP's revenues by product line and total costs broken down into SG&A and Claims & Adjustments for the years 2014, 2015, and 2016.

exhibits.title: 2016 Loss Ratio by Product and Underwriter Information
exhibits.shows: A bar chart showing 2016 loss ratios by product for TTP versus industry average, and a table showing 2016 underwriter headcount, years of experience, and percentage of new hires for TTP versus industry average.

framework: Revenue: Examine premium pricing (has TTP lowered prices to drive volume?) and volume mix (product lines, customer segments) — note volume is clearly not the issue given doubling of premiums
Costs (Variable) — Claims: Is TTP paying out more in claims than usual? Investigate loss ratio trends across product lines
Costs (Fixed) — SG&A: Have fixed operating costs risen disproportionately with growth?
External / Competition: Has the market become more competitive, driving margins down? Are competitors experiencing the same margin issues?

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 1, identify the root cause of the profitability decline. What is driving costs up?
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate or observe that the loss ratio (claims / written premium) has increased from approximately 71% in 2014 (355/500) to 78% in 2015 (585/750) to 80% in 2016 (800/1000). SG&A has grown but is not the primary driver. The key insight is that claims costs are rising faster than revenue, indicating bad underwriting or increased risk. Candidate should identify claims and adjustments as the root cause and ask to explore further.

math.setup: Loss ratio = Claims and adjustments / Total revenue written premium
steps: SG&A as % of revenue: 125/500=25%, 150/750=20%, 190/1000=19% — declining, not the issue
math.answer: Loss ratio has risen from 71% to 80% over 3 years; claims are the root cause of declining profitability.

questions.prompt: Brainstorm potential reasons why TTP's claims costs could be rising.
questions.guidance: Candidate should generate at least 3 reasons before moving to Exhibit 2. Strong answers cover: bad underwriting, a few unusual catastrophic losses, new products that are riskier, increased number of claims, increased severity of claims.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 2, what does the data tell us about the cause of TTP's elevated loss ratios, and which 3 of the 6 product underwriting teams should receive the SpecialtyTrain training to maximize savings and achieve the $40M profit target?
questions.guidance: Candidate should observe: (1) Loss ratios are elevated across all 6 product lines versus industry average — not concentrated in one product. (2) TTP underwriters are far less experienced (3.4 vs 6.9 years) and have a much higher proportion of new hires (43% vs 20%) than the industry — pointing to bad underwriting as the systemic cause. Then candidate should calculate potential savings for each product and select the top 3.

math.setup: For each product: Improvement opportunity = TTP loss ratio - Industry average loss ratio. Potential savings ($M) = Improvement opportunity x 2016 written premium ($M). Select the 3 products with highest potential savings.
steps: Professional Athlete Injury: (81%-75%) x 100 = 6% x 100 = $6M savings
Top 3 by savings: Medical Malpractice ($16M), Pollution ($10.5M), Oil Tankers ($10M) = $36.5M total savings
New total profit: $10M existing + $36.5M savings = $46.5M — exceeds the $40M target
math.answer: Train Medical Malpractice, Pollution, and Oil Tanker underwriting teams. Total savings of $36.5M plus existing $10M profit = $46.5M, exceeding the $40M two-year goal.

brainstorming.prompt: What are potential reasons TTP's claims costs (loss ratio) could be rising?

categories.name: Underwriting quality
ideas: Bad underwriting — policies priced too low for the risk taken on
New hires lacking expertise to assess obscure specialty risks
Rapid hiring pace outstripping training and mentorship capacity

categories.name: Claims frequency and severity
ideas: Increased number of claims filed by insureds
Increased severity of individual claims (larger payouts per event)
Adverse selection — attracting riskier clients due to lower pricing

categories.name: External / market factors
ideas: Catastrophic one-time events (e.g., major oil spill, large natural disaster)
New product lines that are inherently riskier and not yet well-modeled
Macro environment increasing frequency or severity of insured events

categories.name: Operational
ideas: Weak claims management or adjustment processes overpaying claims
Fraud or abuse by claimants going undetected
Insufficient actuarial reserves leading to poor pricing

recommendation: TTP's profitability decline is driven by rising claims costs — the loss ratio increased from 71% to 80% over three years — caused by poor underwriting quality stemming from aggressive hiring of inexperienced underwriters (43% new hires vs. 20% industry average, 3.4 vs. 6.9 years average experience)

Recommend TTP engage SpecialtyTrain to provide supplemental training to the Medical Malpractice, Pollution, and Oil Tankers underwriting teams, which offer $16M, $10.5M, and $10M in savings respectively — totaling $36.5M — bringing projected annual profit to $46.5M and exceeding the $40M two-year target
risks: Training may not be as effective as SpecialtyTrain has guaranteed
Other root causes (e.g., catastrophic losses, adverse selection) may also be contributing to elevated loss ratios and are not addressed by training
Cost of the training program has not been factored in and could reduce net benefit
The three untrained product teams (Natural Disaster, Professional Athlete Injury, Container Ships) will continue to have elevated loss ratios
next_steps: Request a pilot or trial run from SpecialtyTrain on one underwriting team to validate the effectiveness of the training before full commitment
Work with actuaries to audit current underwriting guidelines and ensure pricing adequately reflects risk across all product lines
Evaluate the total cost of the SpecialtyTrain program and model net profit impact
Develop a longer-term plan to train the remaining three underwriting teams in subsequent years
Establish KPIs to track loss ratio by product on a quarterly basis going forward
